newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Police suspect foul play in Philippine hotel fire.
newsitem.headline: Police suspect foul play in Philippine hotel fire.

text.p: A fire that gutted an hotel and killed 25 people in the Philippines' most troubled region may have been deliberate, investigators said on Sunday.
But police have not pinpointed the person or group which might have torched the six-storey Imperial Hotel in Cotabato city on the southern island of Mindanao, they said.
The death toll rose to 25 after firemen recovered the body of another woman from the ruins. Survivors jumped for their lives as flames swept through the three upper floors.

"That (arson) is what is emerging in our investigation. That is our suspicion," Fire Officer Andal Sawil, the fire department spokesman, said by telephone in the largely Moslem city 900 km (560 miles) south of Manila.
The suspicion was based on initial findings that flames apparently broke out at the same time on the three floors, Sawil said. He said fire debris was now being tested in the laboratory.
Asked who might have set the hotel ablaze, Sawil said: "I cannot answer that."
The dead included seven women, three of them pregnant. No foreigners were among the victims, police inspector Jaime Guadilla told Reuters.
But a spokesman for former rebel chief Nur Misuari, who now heads a Moslem autonomous region and whose followers accounted for most of the dead, insisted the fire was an accident.

"(Misuari) ordered a full investigation of the incident to look at all the angles, but at the moment we can categorically say there was no possible sabotage," spokesman Ustadz Murshi Ibrahim told reporters.
"We believe this was a pure act of nature. It was an accident. Please don't place the word sabotage in your reports."
Survivors, 11 of whom broke their legs leaping from the building, complained there was no fire alarm.

Police earlier said the fire, the worst in the country since 152 revellers died in a Manila disco fire just over a year ago, started on the third floor in an unoccupied prayer room, used by both Christians and Moslems.

Saudi Arabian preacher Al Daruis, one of the survivors, said he only found out there was a fire when he phoned the reception desk to complain about the smell of smoke. Staff told him to flee the building.
The fire broke out a day before the hotel was due to host several mainly Islamic diplomats who were to hear Misuari's first state of the region address since taking office last October.
His election came after Misuari signed a peace deal with Manila, ending a 24-year revolt seeking autonomy for the Moslem region within the predominantly Christian Philippines.
Despite the peace pact, an air of mistrust and violence still lingers in Mindanao island.
Political analysts say some members of Moslem rebel groups resent Misuari's rise into the Philippine establishment, while Christians on the island remain deeply suspicious of his rule.
Elsewhere on the island, another Moslem separatist group continues to battle government troops, and more than 30 people have died in an upsurge in violence in the past two weeks.
